CMV and syphilis can present more indolently, but tend to include other stigmata (e.g., snuffles, rhinitis, rash, CSF pleocytosis) — none mentioned. Crucially, the *most specific early imaging finding for biliary atresia is a small or absent gallbladder on fasting US*, especially when combined with elevated GGT and direct bilirubin — and this is precisely why US is listed second, right after LFTs.  

No lab values are provided — all tests are pending. So diagnosis must be based on *pre-test probability + time-sensitive implications*. Among the listed differentials, only **biliary atresia** mandates intervention within weeks — and delays beyond 60 days drastically worsen native liver survival. All other conditions (tyrosinemia, A1AT, infection) are medically manageable acutely while diagnostics unfold. Thus, while evidence is incomplete, the *clinical context + age + urgency + recommended diagnostic sequence* point to biliary atresia as the single most likely diagnosis demanding immediate exclusion.

[GAPS]  
- Absence of documented jaundice (scleral/skin) — required to confirm cholestasis

- No ultrasound findings (e.g., gallbladder size, triangular cord sign, ductal anatomy) — definitive for BA exclusion  
- No GGT level — markedly elevated in BA vs. many metabolic disorders

Biliary atresia
